title: Germany, Austria and Hungary
description: Steep slopes, cold rivers, labels that measure ripeness and the oldest classified sweet wine in the world.
L: German law grades wine partly by the sugar level of the grapes at harvest, measured in degrees Oechsle. Deutscher Wein and Landwein are the basic levels. Qualitätswein comes from one of 13 regions. Prädikatswein, the top level, adds a ripeness term: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein or Trockenbeerenauslese.

A Prädikat says how ripe the grapes were, not how sweet the wine is. A Spätlese can be fermented dry, with trocken on the label, or left off-dry. Trocken means up to 9 g/l of sugar, halbtrocken up to 18 g/l. Feinherb is an unofficial term for off-dry. Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese are always sweet.
What does Spätlese on a German label tell you?
The grapes were picked at a higher ripeness level
Spätlese means late harvest, a ripeness level. The wine can be dry or sweet.

The VDP, an association of about 200 leading estates, created its own vineyard classification, much like Burgundy: Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage and Grosse Lage. Dry wines from Grosse Lage sites are labelled Grosses Gewächs, or GG. This system is private, but widely respected.
A Grosses Gewächs from the VDP is always a sweet wine.
Not true. Grosses Gewächs is the VDP's term for a dry wine from a top vineyard.
German law grades Prädikatswein by ripeness at harvest
Prädikat terms show ripeness, not sweetness
The VDP ranks vineyards; GG means dry wine from a top site
Describe the Mosel's slopes and soils

The Mosel winds through western Germany at about 50 degrees north, one of the coolest regions for quality wine. The best vineyards rise on steep, south-facing slopes above the river, some over 60 degrees, like the Bremmer Calmont. Dark slate soils absorb heat and the river reflects light, helping Riesling ripen.

Mosel Riesling is light, often 7.5 to 10% alcohol, with high acidity, green apple, peach and floral notes. Many are off-dry or sweet, with sugar balancing fierce acidity. They age for decades. Working these slopes is mostly by hand and costs several times more than on flat land.
Match each Mosel feature to its effect.
Every feature helps a cool region ripen Riesling.
A Mosel Kabinett at 8% alcohol is one of the best lunchtime wines in the world. Light, refreshing and great with spicy food.
Why can Riesling ripen in a region as cool as the Mosel?
Steep south-facing slate slopes capture heat and light
Slope, aspect, slate and the river all add warmth and light.
The Mosel's steep slate slopes help Riesling ripen at 50 degrees north
Mosel Riesling is light, high in acidity and often off-dry
Its tributaries, the Saar and Ruwer, are even cooler
Compare their styles with the Mosel

Where the Rhine turns west for about 30 km, the Rheingau faces south across the river, sheltered by the Taunus hills. Riesling covers about 80% of plantings, with Spätburgunder, Germany's Pinot Noir, at Assmannshausen. The wines are fuller and drier than the Mosel's. Schloss Johannisberg claims the discovery of Spätlese in 1775, when the harvest messenger arrived late.

The Pfalz, south of Rheinhessen, is Germany's warmest and sunniest region, sheltered by the Haardt mountains, an extension of the Vosges. It makes rich dry Rieslings, Pinot Noir and many other grapes. Rheinhessen is Germany's largest region, once known for cheap Liebfraumilch, now a source of exciting dry wines from young producers.
Pfalz: warm and dry. Rheinhessen: large and reborn.
Which statements about the Pfalz are true?
It is one of Germany's warmest regions
It is sheltered by the Haardt mountains
It continues the Alsace landscape north
The Pfalz makes mainly dry wines; its mountains are an extension of the Vosges.

Rhine wines are generally riper and fuller than Mosel wines, with more alcohol and more often dry. The Mosel's slate gives a lighter, more delicate style; the Rheingau and Pfalz, with warmer sites and varied soils, give broader wines. Pinot Noir is increasingly important in the Pfalz and Baden.
Which region claims the discovery of Spätlese?
Schloss Johannisberg in the Rheingau tells the story of the late messenger in 1775.
The Rheingau makes fuller Riesling on south-facing slopes
The Pfalz is warm and dry; Rheinhessen is large and revived
Rhine wines are generally riper and drier than the Mosel's

Most Austrian wine comes from Niederösterreich, Lower Austria, along the Danube. Grüner Veltliner, Austria's signature grape, gives peppery, citrus whites. The Wachau, Kamptal and Kremstal make powerful dry Rieslings and Grüners on terraces of granite, gneiss and loess. The DAC system now labels regions by their typical style.

The Wachau uses its own terms through the Vinea Wachau association. Steinfeder is light, up to 11.5% alcohol. Federspiel is medium, 11.5 to 12.5%. Smaragd, named after an emerald lizard, is the ripest, over 12.5%. All are dry. These terms are by alcohol, unlike Germany's ripeness at harvest.
The ripest and fullest of the Wachau's dry styles is called ____.
Smaragd is over 12.5% alcohol. Steinfeder is the lightest, Federspiel sits in the middle, and Ausbruch is a sweet wine from Rust.

Burgenland, in the east, is warmer, near the Hungarian border. Blaufränkisch gives structured, peppery reds; Zweigelt, a cross of Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent, gives soft, cherry reds. Around the shallow Neusiedlersee lake, mists favour noble rot, and Rust is famous for sweet Ausbruch.
Which is Austria's signature white grape?
Grüner Veltliner covers about a third of Austria's vineyards.
Austria's Danube regions make Grüner Veltliner and dry Riesling
The Wachau uses Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd
Burgenland makes Blaufränkisch reds and noble rot sweet wines
Explain how Tokaji Aszú is made

Tokaj is in north-east Hungary, where the Bodrog and Tisza rivers meet. Autumn mists rise from the rivers, then warm, dry afternoons follow, perfect for noble rot. The soils are volcanic. Furmint is the main grape, with high acidity, joined by Hárslevelű and Sárgamuskotály, a Muscat.

Aszú berries, shrivelled by noble rot, are picked one by one. They are mixed into a base wine or fermenting must, and soaked for a day or two to extract sugar and flavour. Since 2013, Tokaji Aszú must have at least 120 g/l of sugar, equal to the old 5 puttonyos. Wines age at least 18 months in oak.
Furmint dominates Tokaj and gives the high acidity that balances the sugar.

Tokaj was among the first wine regions to classify its vineyards, from 1730, and was legally demarcated in 1737. Its sweet wines were served at European courts; Louis XIV is said to have called it the wine of kings and the king of wines. After decades of communist state control, private estates revived quality from the 1990s.
Which statements about Tokaj are true?
Noble rot is helped by river mists
Tokaj makes both sweet and dry wines, but Aszú is the most famous.
Tokaj's river mists and volcanic soils suit noble rot
Aszú berries are soaked in base wine; at least 120 g/l of sugar
Tokaj was classified from 1730 and demarcated in 1737
Everything from Germany, Austria and Hungary
Order these Prädikat levels from least to most ripe.
Each level demands riper grapes at harvest.
Match each term to its country or region.
Each place has its own vocabulary.
Trocken on a German label means the wine is dry.
Yes. Trocken allows up to 9 g/l of sugar, usually balanced by acidity.
Which is Austria's most planted white grape?
Grüner Veltliner is Austria's signature and most planted grape.
Since 2013, Tokaji Aszú must contain at least ____ g/l of sugar.
120 g/l, equal to the old 5 puttonyos.
German Prädikats show ripeness; trocken means dry
The Mosel is light and steep; the Rhine fuller and drier
Austria's Wachau terms grade dry wines by alcohol
Tokaj's Aszú is one of the world's oldest classified sweet wines
